newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco gets its day against FDA.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco gets its day against FDA.

text.p: Tobacco companies are finally getting their day in court Monday against their government foe the Food and Drug Administration, which they accuse of unlawfully trying to control cigarettes.
A record crowd is expected at federal court here to hear the day-long arguments before U.S. District Judge William Osteen, Sr.
The judge is expected to be the first to determine whether the FDA has the right to regulate cigarette sales and marketing and if the proposed rules are constitutional.

Monday's arguments are based on the tobacco industry's motion for summary judgment in which the judge has been asked to make a decision on the merits of the case without a trial. If Osteen feels he needs additional evidence, he will schedule a trial in the near future.

"The tobacco regulations mark the first time in the history of the FDA that the agency has asserted jurisdiction over cigarettes and smokeless tobacco products as customarily marketed," the industry said in its motion.

"That assertion of authority overturns FDA's own settled interpretation of food and drug law dating back to 1914, and violates longstanding reliance by Congress and the tobacco sector of the national economy on the established understanding of the limits of FDA's jurisdiction."

Since the first set of FDA rules is set to take effect on Feb. 28, lawyers believe that Osteen will either make a ruling in the case by that time or perhaps issue a temporary stay on those regulations until a decision is reached.
Regardless of the outcome, it is expected that Osteen's ruling will be appealed to the Fourth Circuit Court of Appeals and most likely to the U.S. Supreme Court.
Battalions of lawyers, tobacco and government officials and reporters began lining up at 6 a.m. to vie for the 200 seats in the federal courthouse here.
Monday's battle dates back to August 1995, when President Bill Clinton authorised the FDA to regulate how cigarettes are sold and marketed in a bid to curb smoking among children.

The FDA rules would ban free samples and billboard ads near schools and playgrounds, limit vending machine sales, ban sponsorship of sports events and the use of cigarette brands on hats, T-shirts and other products.

The rules would restrict advertising in some publications and require retailers to see picture identification for cigarette purchasers under 27 years old. (Eds: CQ) The rules affecting retailers are scheduled to begin Feb. 28.

Virginia, Kentucky and North Carolina, all major tobacco-growing states, have filed court papers urging the court to overturn the regulations. But at least 33 states, along with San Francisco and Guam, are supporting the rules.

The tobacco industry and other plaintiffs will present three main arguments during the hearing. They involve the intent of Congress concerning tobacco regulation, the language and legislative history of the Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act and First Amendment issues.
Osteen could use any of the three arguments to invalidate all of the rules.
